links.passage: Some studies have shown that drip irrigation appears to be consistently more favorable to sugar beet growth than sprinkler irrigation in semi-arid environments (Tognetti et al., 2003).

Other studies indicated that there was no significant difference in the effect of drip irrigation on root length and diameter compared to furrow irrigation, but the root and shoot and plant weights were significantly higher for furrow irrigation (AlJbawi et al., 2021).

Low-frequency micro-irrigation systems (such as subsurface drip irrigation) can maintain stable root zone water tension (-10 to −30 kPa), buffering the impact of irrigation intervals (Camposeo, Rubino, 2003).
supporting_passages: We speculate that the insensitivity of drip irrigation to irrigation intervals and frequencies may be related to its continuous water supply and root adaptation.

Low-frequency micro-irrigation systems (such as subsurface drip irrigation) can maintain stable root zone water tension (-10 to −30 kPa), buffering the impact of irrigation intervals (Camposeo, Rubino, 2003).
links.inference_note: The preceding sentence states that drip yield is insensitive to irrigation intervals and frequencies, and the cited passage gives the buffering of root-zone water tension as the mechanism for this stability of output.

links.passage: Moreover, long-term drip irrigation encourages sugar beets to develop dense, shallow root systems (0–40 cm), which improves water capture efficiency, thereby reducing the influence of irrigation intervals and frequencies (Li et al., 2024).
links.section: Response of effect size to irrigation interval and irrigation frequency

links.passage: As demonstrated by Tognetti et al. in their comparative study of drip versus sprinkler irrigation in semi-arid environments, drip irrigation consistently showed superior efficacy in promoting both sugar beet growth and yield (Tognetti et al., 2003).
